title: Think Like a Researcher
intro: Researchers are trained to let good evidence change their minds. Calabro wants the same from designers — and holds himself to it.

learn.title: “But Google does it” isn't evidence
learn.text:
Google's products are free, pervasive, and can tolerate usability problems most businesses can't. They may succeed **despite** some of their interface choices, not because of them.

Copying a pattern from a dominant product imports the pattern without the market position that absorbs its cost.

try.q: A stakeholder justifies a pattern with “Google does it.” What is the flaw?
options: Google can absorb usability costs others can't
Google's designs are legally protected
Google tests patterns far less than most firms
Google users are more technical than average users
try.explain: Dominance tolerates friction that would cost a smaller business real money.

learn.title: Patterns with decades of evidence against them
learn.text:
Still presented as good ideas:

• Unlabeled icons
• Split buttons
• Placeholder text used as a label
• Floating help and chatbot bubbles
• Info icons hiding key information
• Decorative animation

Calabro offers the list as something to send to a designer who genuinely wants to learn — a starting point, not a rulebook.

try.q: How does Calabro describe his list of evidence-backed articles?
options: A starting point, not a rulebook
The definitive standard for interaction design
A checklist to apply before every release
A replacement for usability testing
try.explain: It is for a designer who genuinely wants to learn.

learn.title: The standard cuts both ways
learn.text:
Don't change your mind because someone says a pattern is bad. **Ask for the evidence, check its method, decide whether it applies to your users.**

And if good research with your actual users shows a “bad” pattern works in your context, the researcher has to update too.

Experience should improve your first judgments, not make them untouchable.

The prompt for the article was a book that changed how Calabro thinks about contextual inquiry — enough that he started piloting the new approach.

try.q: Your research shows a widely criticised pattern works well for your users. What should you do?
options: Update your position — the evidence cuts both ways
Dismiss the result as a sampling artefact
Keep the pattern but don't publish the finding
Run the study again until it matches the literature
try.explain: The same standard applies to researchers.

test.q: What does Calabro say experience should do?
options: Improve your first judgments without making them untouchable
Replace the need to check new evidence
Let you decide design questions faster than juniors
Qualify you to set standards for the whole team
test.explain: Good evidence should still be able to change your mind.

test.q: What should you do when someone tells you a pattern is bad?
options: Ask for the evidence and check its method
Accept it if they are more senior than you
Change the design and move on quickly
Put it to a vote in the next design review
test.explain: Then decide whether the evidence applies to your users.

test.q: Which is on Calabro's list of patterns with evidence against them?
options: Info icons that hide key information
Breadcrumb navigation on deep pages
Inline validation on long forms
Persistent labels above input fields
test.explain: The last two are things he recommends.

test.q: Why did a book prompt this article?
options: Its approach changed how he thinks about contextual inquiry
It disproved several of his earlier articles
It is the only research book he recommends
It was written by a former colleague of his
test.explain: He was piloting the method as a result — learning doing what it should.

test.q: What is the article's view of Google's usability problems?
options: Its products may succeed despite them
They are deliberate experiments on users
They prove usability rules no longer apply
They only affect users outside the United States
test.explain: Free and pervasive products tolerate friction others cannot.
